doc.title: Bill Watrous interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 26, 1999

title: Thad Jones and Bob Rosengarden's Dick Cavett band
summary: He recalls Thad Jones's care and criticism, the intimidating band, and the blowing rehearsals on Rosengarden's Cavett band.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: You seem to have had a pretty special relationship with Thad Jones. What a guy.

He was wonderful. I was devastated when he left New York number one, and number two when I heard he was sick. I didn’t know what to do about it. He wasn’t taking any calls or anything. But I found out. Jerome Richardson told me what a special feeling Thad had for me, and I mean he brought me to tears, literally. He gave me a dressing down every so often too, because I wasn’t assuming my responsibilities when I played on the band right. I was still flaking off occasionally and trying, you know partying and having a good time instead of taking responsibility for what was my due. I wasn’t accepting the responsibility. I was still scared and floundering around a bit. Oh you know, trying to find a way to fit in. Because the band intimidated me, to tell you the truth, it really did. It just went places I never imagined a band could go.

That’s right. And I never forgot that. And when I came off of that band and then started working with Bob Rosengarden’s band on “The Dick Cavett Show,” and that was a very professionally adept ensemble, I would have to say in the studios that was the most adept ensemble I have ever played with. I mean we had great players on there, I mean and they were just taking no prisoners. The band was so clean and so right, and what Rosengarden would do, bless him, is we would go into rehearsal and the first 45 minutes that we were there he would pull stuff out of the library and we would just blow and get it out of our systems. He would open it up and let guys play. Let Eddie Daniels play, let me play, let Virgil Jones play a little bit, and it was a real learning experience. But it was a blowing experience actually. It gave us a release. It wasn’t just a job. We went there and when we went to rehearsal we knew that we were going to play. And when we got through playing then we would go and rehearse the show. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
